name: Aegis
powers: Scatters armies with terror; bears the head of Medusa (gorgoneion).
description: The storm-bearing shield of Zeus, lent to Athena and sometimes Apollo, an aegis of goatskin fringed with gold tassels; in Homer it scatters armies and houses the gorgoneion, the severed head of Medusa. Hephaestus forged its golden version for Zeus. It marks divine protection and terror in Greek epic.
source: Homer, Iliad (with the gorgoneion also in Hesiod and later mythographers)

name: Golden Fleece
maker: The ram Chrysomallus, sent by Hermes
powers: Object of the quest of the Argonauts; hung in the grove of Ares under a dragon's guard.
description: The golden fleece of the winged ram that carried Phrixus and Helle to Colchis; Jason and the Argonauts sailed to retrieve it from the grove of Ares, where a sleepless dragon guarded it. It is the goal of the Argonaut cycle, the price King Aeetes demanded of Jason before he would surrender it.
source: Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica; Apollodorus, Bibliotheca

name: Caduceus
powers: Charm of the herald; conduces the souls of the dead to the underworld; later sign of peace and commerce.
description: Hermes' herald's staff, first described as a rod wrapped with fillets or ribbons and only later twined with serpents; it charmed mortals and spirits and led souls to the underworld. Its winged form becomes the sign of peace and commerce in Roman retellings, recorded in the Homeric Hymn to Hermes.
source: Homeric Hymn to Hermes; later literary and artistic tradition

name: Perseus' Sickle
powers: Could sever the head of Medusa and shear through stone and serpent.
description: The curved sickle-sword, harpe, with which Perseus beheaded the Gorgon Medusa, given to him by Hermes on his quest. Ancient sources describe it as a sword or sickle that could shear through stone and serpent, and the severed head's gaze still petrified his foes. It closes the Medusa episode and arms Athena with the gorgoneion.
source: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca; later iconography

name: Talos
powers: Patrolled Crete hurling rocks at ships; kept a single vein of ichor sealed by a nail at the ankle.
description: Talos, the bronze automaton forged by Hephaestus and given to Minos to patrol the shores of Crete; a giant man of bronze with a single vein of ichor sealed by a nail at the ankle. In the Argonautica he hurls rocks at passing ships until Medea charms him and the plug is drawn, draining his life-fluid.
source: Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica

name: Pandora's Jar
maker: Pandora, created by Hephaestus at Zeus' command
powers: Releases sorrows, sickness, and toil on humankind; hope alone remains inside.
description: The great jar or pithos that Pandora opened, releasing sorrows and evils upon humankind and keeping hope trapped inside, in Hesiod's Works and Days; the familiar 'box' is a later Latin mistranslation of pithos. Given to Epimetheus as Zeus' gift, it explains the origin of toil, sickness, and death in Greek myth.
source: Hesiod, Works and Days

name: Sword of Theseus
maker: Aegeus (left beneath the rock at Troezen)
powers: Proof of royal birth; recognizes Theseus to his father Aegeus at Athens.
description: The sword of the Athenian hero Theseus, left with a pair of sandals beneath a great rock at Troezen by his father Aegeus; when Theseus grew strong enough to lift the rock, the tokens proved his royal birth, and he carried the sword to Athens, where his father recognized him by it. Plutarch and Pausanias record the tokens.
source: Plutarch, Life of Theseus; Pausanias, Description of Greece

name: Lyre of Orpheus
maker: Gift of Apollo or Hermes to Orpheus
powers: Charmed beasts, trees, and stones; moved the dead and soothed Cerberus.
description: The lyre of Orpheus, a gift from Apollo or Hermes with the power to charm beasts, trees, and stones and to move the dead; its music soothed Cerberus and won Hades' consent to let Eurydice return, a bargain lost when Orpheus looked back. After his death the lyre was set among the stars.
source: Ovid, Metamorphoses; Apollodorus, Bibliotheca

name: Trident of Poseidon
powers: Shakes the earth, splits cliffs, raises and calms storms; struck rock to produce the spring on the Acropolis.
description: The three-pronged trident of Poseidon, forged by the Cyclopes, that shakes the earth, splits cliffs, and raises or calms storms; with it he struck the rock of the Acropolis to produce a salt spring in his contest with Athena. It is the standard emblem of sea power and earthquakes in Greek myth.
source: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca; Homeric Hymn to Poseidon

name: Robe of Nessus
maker: Deianeira, using the centaur Nessus' poisoned blood
powers: Loved as a charm; in truth burned Heracles so terribly that he sought death by fire.
description: The robe or tunic smeared with the centaur Nessus' blood that Deianeira gave Heracles, believing it a love charm; the poisoned blood burned Heracles so terribly he begged to be burned on a pyre. Sophocles' Women of Trachis makes the robe the instrument of the hero's death.
source: Sophocles, Women of Trachis

name: Shield of Achilles
material: Bronze, tin, gold, silver with enamelled core
powers: Depicts the whole cosmos: earth, sea, sky, two cities, war, peace, and the encircling Ocean; impenetrable in battle.
description: The shield Hephaestus forged for Achilles, described at length in the Iliad: a five-layered shield with scenes of earth, sea, sky, sun, moon, two cities, a lawsuit, war, farming, harvest, and dance, all framed by Ocean. It is the archetype of the crafted cosmic artifact in Greek epic.
source: Homer, Iliad (Book 18)

name: Robe of Medea
material: Robed cloth and a golden diadem, steeped in poison
powers: Bursts into flame on the wearer; destroys Glauce and her father Creon.
description: The poisoned robe and golden diadem Medea sent to Glauce, Jason's new bride at Corinth; when the princess donned them, fire consumed her and her father Creon. Euripides' Medea makes the bridal gifts the engine of her revenge, and the robe recurs as a deadly bridal-gift motif in later myth.
source: Euripides, Medea

name: Bridle of Bellerophon
maker: Brought by Athena in a dream
powers: Tamed the winged horse Pegasus so Bellerophon could ride it against the Chimera.
description: The golden bridle Athena gave Bellerophon to tame the winged horse Pegasus, allowing him to ride and, mounted, to defeat the fire-breathing Chimera; Apollodorus tells of the dream in which Athena brought the bridle, and Pausanias describes the shrine at Corinth where it was dedicated.
source: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca; Pausanias, Description of Greece

name: Wings of Daedalus
material: Feathers bound with wax and thread
powers: Carried Daedalus and Icarus off Crete; deadly when the wax melts in the sun's heat.
description: The feathered wings Daedalus built from wax and thread for himself and his son Icarus to escape the labyrinth of Crete; Icarus flew too near the sun, the wax melted, and he fell into the sea. Ovid's Metamorphoses gives the fullest telling, and the wings became the symbol of doomed invention.
source: Ovid, Metamorphoses (Book 8)

name: Bow of Odysseus
material: Polished wood with horn tip (gift of Iphitus)
maker: Given to Odysseus by Iphitus; strung only by its owner
powers: Shot an arrow through twelve axe heads; brought death to the suitors of Ithaca.
description: The great bow of Odysseus, which he alone could string and shoot through twelve axe-heads; Penelope's contest of the bow is the test of her suitors, and Odysseus slays them with it on his return to Ithaca in the Odyssey. Its unyielding strength stands for the hero's unchallenged identity.
source: Homer, Odyssey (Book 21)

name: Crown of Ariadne
powers: Set among the stars as the constellation Corona Borealis after Ariadne's death.
description: The golden crown Ariadne wore when Theseus rescued her from Crete; Dionysus later set it in the heavens as the constellation Corona Borealis. Catullus and later poets tell how the crown commemorates the abandoned bride of Naxos, transformed into a circlet of stars.
source: Catullus, Carmen 64; Apollodorus, Bibliotheca

name: Shield of Aeneas
powers: Shows the future of Rome, from Romulus to the triumph of Augustus at Actium.
description: The shield Vulcan forged for Aeneas, engraved with the future of Rome: Romulus and Remus, the rape of the Sabines, and the triumph of Augustus at Actium. Virgil describes it at the close of Aeneid 8 as the destiny of the Trojan line made visible in bronze.
source: Virgil, Aeneid (Book 8)

name: Sibylline Books
powers: Prophetic verses consulted by the Roman state to avert calamities; their burning punished Tarquin's haggling.
description: The nine books of prophetic verses the Cumaean Sibyl offered to Tarquinius Superbus, of which she burned six and sold the last three at the original price, as Livy and Dionysius of Halicarnassus relate; kept in the temple of Jupiter, the surviving Sibylline Books were consulted for Rome's most dangerous crises.
source: Livy, History of Rome; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Roman Antiquities

name: Lituus of Romulus
powers: Marked the regions of the sky for augury at Rome's foundation; found unharmed after the burning of the Curia Saliorum.
description: The curved augur's staff with which Romulus marked out the regions of the sky when founding Rome; kept in the Curia Saliorum on the Palatine, it was found unharmed after the temple burned, a portent of Rome's safety. Cicero and Plutarch record the relic, and augurs carried the lituus as the mark of their office.
source: Cicero, De Divinatione; Plutarch, Life of Camillus; Dionysius of Halicarnassus

name: Ancile
maker: Fell from heaven in the reign of Numa; copies made by the smith Mamurius Veturius
powers: Pledge of Rome's eternity; twelve copies kept the true shield hidden from thieves.
description: The sacred shield of Mars that fell from heaven in the reign of Numa, taken as a pledge of Rome's eternity; Numa had eleven identical copies made so that thieves could not identify it, and the Salii guarded and carried all twelve in the March procession. Plutarch, Ovid, and Servius tell the legend.
source: Plutarch, Life of Numa; Ovid, Fasti (Book 3); Servius, on the Aeneid

name: Golden Bough
maker: Hidden in the wood of Proserpina
powers: Admitted a living man into the underworld; the offering Proserpina required of Aeneas.
description: The golden bough Aeneas plucked in the Sibyl's wood to gain entry to the underworld and offer to Proserpina; like mistletoe it must be found and plucked by fate alone, and its presence admits the living to the realm of the dead. Virgil makes it the passport of the Aeneid's descent.
source: Virgil, Aeneid (Book 6)

name: Arrows of Cupid
powers: The golden arrow kindles love; the blunt leaden one drives love away.
description: The arrows of Cupid in Ovid's Metamorphoses: the golden-headed shaft that kindles love and the blunt leaden one that drives love away. Apollo, struck by the golden, chases Daphne, who flees because of the leaden; the two arrows explain uncontrollable passion in Roman myth.
source: Ovid, Metamorphoses (Book 1)

name: Sword of Damocles
maker: Hung at the court of Dionysius II of Syracuse
powers: Showed Damocles the peril hidden in royal ease; the emblem of insecurity in power.
description: The sword suspended by a single horse-hair over the head of Damocles, courtier of Dionysius II of Syracuse, to show him the insecurity of royal power; when Damocles envied the tyrant's life, Dionysius made him taste it, and the hanging sword became the emblem of peril in high office. Told by Cicero in the Tusculan Disputations.
source: Cicero, Tusculan Disputations

name: Corona Civica
material: Oak leaves (holm, esculent, or common oak)
powers: Rewarded a soldier who saved a fellow citizen's life in battle and held the ground; granted lifelong honour and the right to sit with senators.
description: The Roman civic crown of oak leaves, second only to the grass crown in honour, awarded to a soldier who saved a fellow citizen's life in battle and held the ground; the inscription 'ob cives servatos' and the right to wear it for life made it Rome's most coveted decoration, described by Pliny and Aulus Gellius.
source: Pliny the Elder, Natural History (Book 16); Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights (Book 5)

name: Liver of Piacenza
powers: Model of a sheep's liver used in hepatoscopy; its sixteen inscribed zones map the heavens onto the organ.
description: The life-sized bronze model of a sheep's liver, found near Piacenza in 1877 and dated to the late 2nd-early 1st century BC, its surface divided into sixteen inscribed zones naming Etruscan gods; used by haruspices to teach and perform hepatoscopy, reading the future from the liver's form. It is the key artifact of Etruscan divination.
source: Archaeological find (Gossolengo, 1877; Museo Civico di Palazzo Farnese, Piacenza)

name: Pyrgi Gold Plaques
maker: Dedicated by Thefarie Velianas of Caere
powers: Bilingual dedicatory texts linking the Etruscan goddess Uni with the Phoenician Astarte; cornerstone of Etruscan language study.
description: Three gold sheets found in 1964 at the Etruscan port of Pyrgi, inscribed about 500 BC in Etruscan and Phoenician, recording Thefarie Velianas' dedication of Temple B to Uni, identified with Astarte; the bilingual text is one of the oldest historical documents from Italy and a cornerstone for understanding the Etruscan language.
source: Archaeological find (Pyrgi, Santa Severa, 1964; Museo Nazionale Etrusco di Villa Giulia, Rome)

name: Tizona
material: Iron and steel blade with silver-gilt hilt
maker: Blade of Andalusian manufacture, c. 11th century
powers: Sword of El Cid won from King Yucef of Valencia; 'worth a thousand marks of gold' in the Cantar.
description: The sword Tizona, named in the Cantar de Mio Cid as El Cid's blade won from King Yucef of Valencia; the sword shown in the Museo de Burgos has an 11th-century blade, though its hilt and inscriptions are later additions, so its link to Rodrigo Diaz de Vivar rests on legend rather than proof.
source: Cantar de Mio Cid; Museo de Burgos (provenance and metallurgical studies)

name: Chest of El Cid
powers: A ruse: sand offered as treasure to raise funds from the moneylenders Rachel and Vidas.
description: The chest of El Cid in the Cantar de Mio Cid, filled with sand, pawned to the moneylenders Rachel and Vidas as a supposed hoard of treasure to raise funds for exile; the ruse displays the hero's cunning and was never meant to be redeemed, a famous comic episode of the Spanish epic.
source: Cantar de Mio Cid

name: Santo Caliz
material: Agate cup with gold mounts, pearls, and gems
era: Agate cup of the 2nd-1st century BC; mounts medieval
maker: Unknown Hellenistic or Roman lapidary; goldwork by later craftsmen
powers: Venerated as the cup of the Last Supper; its identification is tradition, not verified history.
description: The Holy Chalice of Valencia, an agate cup of the 2nd-1st century BC set in medieval gold mounts, kept in Valencia Cathedral since 1437; tradition identifies it as the cup of the Last Supper, brought from Jerusalem via Rome and Huesca, but that identification cannot be verified and is disputed. The cup itself is genuine and ancient.
source: Valencia Cathedral tradition; A. Beltran, archaeological study (1960)

name: Rooster of Barcelos
material: Legendary roast fowl; modern ceramic replicas
powers: A roasted rooster rose and crowed to prove a condemned pilgrim's innocence.
description: The Rooster of Barcelos, from the Portuguese legend of a Galician pilgrim wrongly condemned to hang in Barcelos; before the judge, the pilgrim swore his innocence by the roasted rooster on the table, and the bird rose and crowed. The miracle saved him, and the ceramic Galo de Barcelos became a national symbol.
source: Portuguese oral tradition; collected versions of the Barcelos legend

name: Nau Catrineta
era: Folk era (legend set in the Age of Sail)
powers: Lost at sea until an angel saved the captain and the ship reached port.
description: The legendary ship of the Portuguese romance 'Nau Catrineta', lost at sea for seven years until the crew drew lots to sacrifice the captain-general; the devil, disguised as the lookout, demanded his soul, but an angel saved him and the ship reached port. Recorded in Almeida Garrett's Romanceiro, the ballad survives in many oral versions.
source: Portuguese oral tradition; Almeida Garrett, Romanceiro

name: Portuguese Guitar
material: Wood, metal strings (twelve strings in six courses)
maker: Developed from the English cittern in Lisbon
powers: The signature voice of fado, said to express saudade itself.
description: The Portuguese guitar, a twelve-string cittern with a pear-shaped body, the defining instrument of fado; its bright, plaintive sound accompanies the singer in Lisbon's taverns and is said to voice saudade itself. A documented tradition of urban song rather than a mythic relic, it anchors Portugal's musical folklore.
source: Ethnographic and musicological documentation of the fado tradition

name: Nazar Boncugu
powers: Deflects the envious gaze of the nazar (evil eye).
description: The nazar boncugu, the blue-and-white glass evil-eye bead of Turkey, worn as jewellery or hung in homes and on vehicles to deflect the envious gaze of the nazar; its counter-charm is a documented folk practice tied to the Mediterranean belief in the evil eye, and it remains the most widespread Turkish protective amulet.
source: Turkish folk practice; ethnographic documentation

name: Karagoz
material: Dyed translucent leather (camel hide) on a stick
powers: Comic everyman of the shadow screen, bickering with Hacivat in plays performed behind a lit panel.
description: Karagoz, the shadow puppet of Ottoman Turkish theatre, a comic everyman who bickers with his friend Hacivat in the traditional play; the translucent leather puppets are worked behind a lit screen and the whole form takes its name from the main character, said to have been an ironworker whose antics amused the Sultan. A living oral-dramatic tradition of Turkey.
source: Turkish oral tradition and documented Ottoman shadow theatre

name: Talismanic Shirt
material: Cotton or linen, painted with ink and gold
powers: Worn next to the skin to shield the wearer from wounds, illness, and evil in battle.
description: The tilsimli gomlek, or talismanic shirt, a cotton garment painted with Qur'anic verses, magic squares, and astrological signs, worn next to the skin by Ottoman sultans for protection in battle; some eighty survive in the Topkapi collection, including Cem Sultan's shirt begun in 1477, whose astrological moment of making is inscribed in it.
source: Topkapi Palace Museum collection; Tezcan, Tilsimli Gomlekler

name: Mehter Davul
material: Wooden shell with skin heads, struck with a beater
powers: Beats the rhythm of the janissary march, inspiring troops and intimidating the enemy.
description: The great bass drum of the mehter, the Ottoman military band, slung and struck to beat the rhythm of the janissary march; its booming sound, with the zurna, was meant to inspire troops and terrify the enemy in battle, and the mehter davul remains an emblem of Ottoman martial music.
source: Ottoman musical tradition; documentation of the mehter band

name: Luzzu
era: Traditional working boat (modern form early 20th century)
maker: Maltese boatwrights, family yards at Marsaxlokk and Gozo
powers: The painted Eye of Osiris on the prow wards off the evil eye and guides the boat home.
description: The luzzu, the brightly painted wooden fishing boat of the Maltese islands, whose prow carries a pair of apotropaic eyes known as the Eye of Osiris or of Horus, an inheritance from Phoenician seafaring meant to ward off the evil eye and guide the boat home; the working fleets of Marsaxlokk still sail with the painted gaze.
source: Ethnographic and maritime documentation of the Maltese fishing tradition

name: Ivory Statue of Galatea
powers: Brought to life by Aphrodite at Pygmalion's prayer; became his wife.
description: The ivory statue the sculptor Pygmalion of Cyprus carved and fell in love with; at his prayer Aphrodite brought it to life as Galatea, who became his wife. Ovid's Metamorphoses tells the story, the classic tale of art animated by desire, and it is set on the island of Cyprus.
source: Ovid, Metamorphoses (Book 10)
